Algeria.polity: Byzantine Africa and independent Moorish (Berber) kingdoms
Algeria.summary: From the 5th century, Berber chiefs known at the time as Moorish kings ruled small states both outside and inside the former Roman provinces: Masuna, known from an inscription at Altava in Mauretania Caesariensis, and, in the Byzantine period, Iaudas in the Aures. Byzantine territory in Africa was governed from Carthage, where Emperor Maurice (r. 582-602) created an exarchate in a land occupied largely by Berbers.

sources.title: G. Camps, Rex gentium Maurorum et Romanorum. Recherches sur les royaumes de Mauretanie des VIe et VIIe siecles (Antiquites africaines 20, 1984)

Libya.polity: Byzantine Tripolitania and Cyrenaica; Fezzan, former land of the Garamantes
Libya.summary: Justinian's reconquest of 533-534 began with an anti-Vandal revolt in Tripolitania, backed by Roman soldiers from Cyrenaica, and returned the coast to the empire. Inland lay Fezzan, the old territory of the Garamantes, which the Arabs conquered in 666. Arab armies reached the coast in the 640s; excavations show that Tocra in Cyrenaica stayed inhabited after the conquest. Sources for 570-632 itself are scarce.

sources.title: A. M. Buzaian, Excavations at Tocra (1985-1992) (Libyan Studies 31, 2000)

Morocco.polity: Local Romano-Berber communities outside imperial rule
Morocco.summary: The Roman army had abandoned the southern part of Mauretania Tingitana, including Volubilis, after Diocletian's reorganisation of 285. At Volubilis a cemetery near the Arch of Caracalla has yielded Christian Latin funerary inscriptions dated 599-655 CE, showing a Christianised Romano-Berber population that still used Latin. Islamisation was under way there before Idris I arrived in the late 8th century.

events.t: Christian Latin epitaphs at Volubilis, dated 599-655 CE, attest a Christianised Romano-Berber community still using Latin.

Tunisia.summary: Carthage was the centre of Byzantine Africa. In the late 6th century Emperor Maurice (r. 582-602) made it an exarchate whose governor held military and civil power. In 610 Heraclius, son of the governor of Carthage of the same name, led a fleet to Constantinople, where Phocas was overthrown and Heraclius proclaimed emperor. Amid later defeats he considered moving his capital to Carthage.

events.t: Emperor Maurice (r. 582-602) establishes the exarchate of Carthage, its exarch holding military and civil power; the exact date is uncertain.
Heraclius, son of the governor of Carthage, leads a fleet to Constantinople; Phocas is overthrown and dies on 5 October, and Heraclius becomes emperor.
After heavy losses to Persia, Heraclius considers moving his capital to Carthage but is persuaded to stay by Bishop Sergios of Constantinople and the people.

W. Sahara.summary: This territory, made up of the regions of Rio de Oro and Saguia el-Hamra, lies on the Atlantic between Morocco, Algeria and Mauritania. The sources consulted give no written or dated archaeological evidence about its people or rulers in 570-632.

Mauritania.polity: Soninke communities in the south (early Ghana / Wagadu)
Mauritania.summary: The Ghana (Wagadu) empire, which Britannica dates from the 7th to the 13th century, lay between the Sahara and the headwaters of the Senegal and Niger rivers, in what is now southeastern Mauritania and part of Mali. Its founders were the Soninke. Evidence for 570-632 itself is very thin.

events.t: The Soninke state of Ghana (Wagadu), dated by Britannica from the 7th century, may be taking shape in the southern Sahel.

Sudan.polity: Nubian kingdoms: Nobadia, Makuria and Alodia (Alwa)
Sudan.summary: Three Christian Nubian kingdoms lined the Nile: Nobadia in the north (capital Pachoras, modern Faras), Makuria (capital Dongola) and Alodia (capital Soba). All converted in the 6th century. Nobadia's ruler adopted Miaphysite (Monophysite) Christianity, while John of Biclaro records Makuria's conversion to the Diophysite faith c. 570. Nobadia and Makuria later merged, sometime in the 7th century or by the early 8th.

events.t: The missionary Longinus, successor of Julian, begins work in Nubia; by 575 the three Nubian kingdoms have been converted to Christianity.
John of Biclaro records the conversion of Makuria to the Diophysite (Chalcedonian) faith, c. 570.

sources.title: Nubian Kingdoms
sources.publisher: Nubian Monasteries project, Polish Centre of Mediterranean Archaeology, University of Warsaw

S. Sudan.summary: The swamps and savannas of the upper Nile were inhabited, but no written records exist for this period and archaeological research is very limited, so the societies of the region cannot be described with confidence.

Eritrea.polity: Kingdom of Aksum (Red Sea coast and highlands)
Eritrea.summary: The coast lay within the Christian kingdom of Aksum, whose port Adulis, on the Gulf of Zula, linked African, Mediterranean and Asian trade. Adulis declined as trade routes shifted and was cut off from Mediterranean trade by the rise of Arab powers in the 7th and 8th centuries. Across the Red Sea, Sasanian Persia drove Ethiopian forces from Yemen in the later 6th century.

events.t: A Sasanian expedition sent by Khosrow I expels Ethiopian forces from Yemen; sources date it variously, including 575-576 and 582.
Muslim emigrants from Arabia find protection in the Christian Aksumite kingdom (the First Hijra).
Adulis declines as Red Sea trade shifts and Arab powers rise in the 7th and 8th centuries; the exact chronology is uncertain.

Eritrea.link: The first Muslim emigrants (the First Hijra, 615 CE) were granted protection by the Aksumite kingdom, whose Red Sea coast and port of Adulis lay here.

sources.title: Arabia ii. The Sasanians and Arabia
Negash (Al-Nejashi) Village: Sanctuary of the First Hijra (Tentative List)

Ethiopia.polity: Kingdom of Aksum (ruler known in Islamic tradition as al-Najashi, Ashama)
Ethiopia.summary: Aksum was a Christian kingdom, one of the first to adopt Christianity in the 4th century, and a link between African, Mediterranean and Asian trade. Its rule in Yemen ended when Sasanian Persia expelled Ethiopian forces in the later 6th century. According to Islamic sources, its ruler, the Negus Ashama (al-Najashi), sheltered Muslim emigrants from Arabia, among them Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, from c. 615.

events.t: First Hijra: Muslim emigrants from Arabia are granted protection by the Christian Aksumite kingdom.
Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and the remaining emigrants in Ethiopia rejoin Muhammad ﷺ at the time of the conquest of Khaybar, per Sahih al-Bukhari.
The Negus Ashama dies (date uncertain); per Sahih al-Bukhari, Muhammad ﷺ announced his death and led the funeral prayer for him.

Ethiopia.link: According to Islamic sources, the Negus Ashama (al-Najashi) sheltered Muslim emigrants from c. 615, including Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, and Muhammad ﷺ led the funeral prayer for him when he died.

sources.title: Negash (Al-Nejashi) Village: Sanctuary of the First Hijra (Tentative List)

Djibouti.summary: This coast lies on the Bab el-Mandeb strait on the northeast coast of the Horn of Africa. The sources consulted give no written or dated archaeological evidence about its people or rulers in 570-632.

Somalia.summary: The sources consulted say little about the Somali coast in this period. Britannica describes Seylac (Zeila), on the Gulf of Aden in the far north-west, as the most important Arab settlement on the Somali coast only from the 9th century, trading between Christian Ethiopia and Muslim Arabia. Evidence for 570-632 is very limited.

Somaliland.summary: Seylac (Zeila), on the Gulf of Aden, became the most important Arab settlement on the Somali coast from the 9th century, a centre of trade between Christian Ethiopia and Muslim Arabia in ivory, skins and incense. What this coast was like in 570-632 is not documented in the sources consulted.

Kenya.polity: Coastal and hinterland communities of the early Tana Tradition
Kenya.summary: From about 600 CE, sites across eastern Africa, including the Kenyan coast, share locally made pottery known as the early Tana Tradition or Triangular-Incised Ware. Its recognition has led archaeologists to stress the indigenous roots of the later cosmopolitan Swahili coastal culture. Evidence for the period is archaeological.

events.t: Sites across eastern Africa are characterised by early Tana Tradition (Triangular-Incised Ware) pottery, c. 600-900.

sources.title: Fleisher and Wynne-Jones, Ceramics and the Early Swahili: Deconstructing the Early Tana Tradition (2011)

Tanzania.summary: Early coastal villages were forerunners of Swahili culture. On Zanzibar, Unguja Ukuu was settled from the 7th, if not the 6th, century and was tied to Indian Ocean trade from its earliest levels. On Pemba, the trading village of Tumbe dates to c. 600-950 and may have produced shell beads for export. Evidence is archaeological.

events.t: Unguja Ukuu on Zanzibar is occupied as a trading settlement from the 7th, if not the 6th, century; its start date is debated.

sources.title: Fitton and Wynne-Jones, Understanding the layout of early coastal settlement at Unguja Ukuu, Zanzibar (2017)
Fleisher and LaViolette, The early Swahili trade village of Tumbe, Pemba Island, Tanzania, AD 600-950 (2013)

Madagascar.summary: The Malagasy language is related to Ma'anyan of southern Borneo, and Malagasy people have both Southeast Asian and African ancestry. When Austronesian seafarers arrived is debated: estimates range from the middle of the first millennium CE to the 7th-8th centuries, and Southeast Asian crops found at early sites give the first archaeological evidence of their presence.

events.t: Austronesian settlers may be reaching Madagascar, estimated on linguistic grounds at about the 7th-8th centuries; dates remain debated.

sources.title: Crowther et al., Ancient crops provide first archaeological signature of the westward Austronesian expansion (2016)
Kusuma et al., Contrasting Linguistic and Genetic Origins of the Asian Source Populations of Malagasy (2016)

Mozambique.summary: Farming communities with decorated pottery and iron-working had settled the coast of southern Mozambique in earlier centuries. In the later first millennium, the beach site of Chibuene was a landing place for Indian Ocean goods; its community supplied imported beads to interior sites such as Schroda. Evidence is archaeological.

sources.title: Sinclair, Ekblom and Wood, Trade and society on the south-east African coast in the later first millennium AD: the case of Chibuene (2012)
Lander & Russell, The archaeological evidence for the appearance of pastoralism and farming in southern Africa (PLoS ONE 13, 2018)

Chad.polity: Sao communities of the Lake Chad basin
Chad.summary: The Sao, the oldest known civilisation of the Lake Chad region, settled around the lake by about the 5th century (one UNESCO text says 5th century BC; the date is disputed). They lived mainly from fishing, hunting and farming, left rich pottery, and are regarded as ancestors of the Kotoko. The period 570-632 is known only through archaeology.

events.t: Sao communities fish, hunt and farm around Lake Chad and produce rich pottery.

Niger.polity: Bura culture of the Niger valley
Niger.summary: In the Niger River valley, the Bura culture buried its dead in terracotta funerary jars topped with figures. The Met dates Bura grave markers to the 3rd-11th centuries, and the UNESCO tentative listing places use of the Bura necropolis between the 3rd and 13th centuries. Bura holds the oldest terracotta equestrian figures in the Niger basin. Evidence is archaeological only.

events.t: The Bura necropolis, used between the 3rd and 13th centuries, receives burials in terracotta jars topped with figures.

Mali.polity: Djenne-Djeno and Inland Niger Delta settlements; possible early Ghana (Wagadu)
Mali.summary: Djenne, inhabited since about 250 BCE, includes the archaeological site of Djenne-Djeno, part of a UNESCO World Heritage property. Excavations there revealed a pre-Islamic urban settlement of circular and rectangular earthen buildings, funerary jars, pottery and metal slag. To the north-west, the Soninke state of Ghana (Wagadu), dated by Britannica from the 7th century, may have been forming.

events.t: Soninke communities may be organising the early Ghana (Wagadu) state, which Britannica dates from the 7th century.
